[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] Amazon Web Services began as an internal Amazon project in July 2002, launched Simple Queue Service in 2004, then reached its modern form with S3 in March 2006 and EC2 in August 2006. It operates as a business segment of Amazon.com, Inc., a public company trading as AMZN, SEC filer CIK 0001018724, headquartered at 410 Terry Avenue North in Seattle, Washington.

As of the source date, AWS states its cloud spans 124 Availability Zones across 39 geographic regions worldwide, with 7 more Availability Zones and 2 more regions, in Saudi Arabia and Chile, announced but not yet live. Within the United States, AWS names Northern Virginia, Ohio, Northern California, and Oregon as public regions, plus two GovCloud regions serving government workloads. The registry here tracks 243 AWS facilities across seven states, California, Mississippi, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Virginia, with the largest concentration in Northern Virginias Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties, the corridor widely known as Data Center Alley.

Amazon has disclosed specific investment figures for Virginia: $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenditure from 2011 through 2021, an additional $35 billion planned for data center campuses through 2040, and $8.2 billion in GDP contribution over the 2011 to 2021 period. The company reported paying $334 million in business personal property taxes in 2022 and employing 8,710 people supporting Virginia data center operations in 2021. Amazon also states it has built or contracted 18 solar farms in Virginia, stated to generate enough power to serve about 276,000 homes.

These figures describe AWSs own reported investment and power posture in its largest US buildout state, not facility by facility specifications. Virginias position as AWSs most concentrated US buildout, backed by declared multi decade capital commitments and utility scale solar contracting, is a direct instance of the compute, power, and buildings link this site tracks: cloud capacity growth here is paired with explicit, dollar denominated grid and land investment rather than compute alone. This facility is recorded under the operator name Amazon Web Services us-east-2 datacenter in this registry, referring to part of the AWS us-east-2 (Ohio) region infrastructure operated by Amazon Web Services. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
This facility is an Amazon Web Services data center in Franklin County, Ohio, part of the us-east-2 region. The operator publishes no power capacity, computing density, or PUE for this site, making its scale relative to AI workloads impossible to assess from available data. Mapped facilities in Ohio number 76, but only eight publish power figures, totaling 60.4 MW across the state, so the absence of a specification here is consistent with sparse public disclosure in the region.

Without published megawatts, computing capacity cannot be estimated. No power generation, cooling technology, or grid interconnection details are disclosed. The site's location in Franklin County places it outside the operator's largest US buildout in Northern Virginia, where AWS has committed $35 billion through 2040 and contracted utility-scale solar; whether similar power procurement or renewable contracting backs this Ohio facility is not published.

The facility cannot be ranked against other Ohio sites by capacity. AWS operates the us-east-2 region across the state as part of its 39 global regions and 124 availability zones, but operator disclosure of site-level power or compute resources remains the exception rather than the rule in this registry. Unless the operator publishes specifications, this campus remains mapped but unmeasurable in the context of AI infrastructure scaling.
